# SK3009 — Review explicitly unsynchronized Lazy in static state

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A static Lazy<T> field initializer explicitly disables thread safety.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Async |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |

## Why

Lazy<T> is thread-safe by default. Passing false or LazyThreadSafetyMode.None explicitly removes that protection; storing that instance in static state warrants review of its access policy. Adding synchronization changes factory execution and exception behavior, so there is no automatic fix.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
static readonly Lazy<object> Cache = new(() => new object(), false);
```

Write:

```csharp
static readonly Lazy<object> Cache = new(() => new object());
```

## When it does not fire

Only direct framework Lazy<T> constructors in static field initializers with constant false or LazyThreadSafetyMode.None are reported. Default constructors, true, PublicationOnly, ExecutionAndPublication, instance fields, ThreadStatic fields, nonconstant modes, derived or user-defined Lazy types and factory methods are excluded. Source constants must be in the same file, including transitive initializers. Static storage is a sharing risk, not proof of concurrent access: deliberate single-threaded access or external synchronization can justify suppression. Constructor assignments and static properties are outside the initial scope.

## Configuration

- `dotnet_diagnostic.SK3009.severity`
